title: Wheat Ridge Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Wheat Ridge wells have a 30-foot median depth. Compare reported yields, water levels, drilling costs and property checks before buying or building.
h1: Wheat Ridge wells: shallow records, site-specific decisions
intro_html:
A shallow well record does not automatically mean a cheap, dependable household supply. Within 5 miles of Wheat Ridge, Colorado DWR records include 9,473 permitted wells, with 5,319 recorded as constructed. Monitoring accounts for 42% of the use mix, compared with 39% domestic/household, so the local statistics are not a clean sample of residential wells.

The search area also reaches toward Lakeside, Mountain View, Edgewater, Fairmount, Applewood and East Pleasant View. Use these figures to frame your questions, then compare wells close to the actual parcel with similar geology and permitted uses.

sections.heading: Why Wheat Ridge’s 30-foot median needs context
sections.html:
Among 5,423 records reporting depth, the median is 30 feet, and the middle half runs from 20–70 feet. That gives a driller a shallow starting reference, not a promised completion depth. With monitoring wells prominent in the records, a household-well bid needs closer comparisons than the area-wide median.

Depths extend well beyond that shallow cluster: 80% are under 100 feet, but the 90th percentile is 264 feet and the deepest reported well is 1,760 feet. Permit aquifer labels include Alluvial, Denver and unnamed/fractured-bedrock entries. Ask the driller which formation the proposed well would target and how that changes footage, casing and grout requirements.

sections.heading: Reported Wheat Ridge yields center on 10 gpm
sections.html:
Only 407 records report pump yield, so this is a much smaller sample than the depth data. The median is 10.0 gpm, with the middle half at 7.0–14.0 gpm. A reported yield in that range is encouraging for household planning, but it does not establish sustained production through changing seasons or authorize outdoor watering.

Low production still matters: 3% report under 1 gpm, and 9% fall in the 1–5 gpm category. For a buyer, that means checking the pumping test rather than relying on a faucet demonstration. A low-yield well may need storage and careful demand management; a larger pump cannot create more groundwater.

sections.heading: Water levels do not show a steady local decline
sections.html:
The 161 records with static water levels show a median depth to water of 13 feet, with the middle half at 10–23 feet. Static level means the resting water level in the well, not the bottom of the hole or the level while pumping. Shallow standing water alone does not establish a dependable supply.

Decade medians are 15 feet in the 1950s, 18 in the 1960s, 95 in the 1970s, 14 in the 2010s and 11 in the 2020s. This series does not show a steady dropping water table. These are grouped measurements from different wells, not repeated readings from a consistent monitoring network.

sections.heading: Wheat Ridge’s permit history is not a contractor roster
sections.html:
Permit issuance reached 1,766 in the 2000s, following 1,532 in the 1990s. Records show 1,180 in the 2010s and 484 in the 2020s, with the newest permit dated 2025. The current decade is incomplete, and permits do not necessarily represent completed household wells.

The most frequent driller-field entry is “Authorized (Pe, Pg)” at 2,573 records; treat that as a record label, not a conventional drilling-company recommendation. Named firms include Adams Water Well Drilling (Adams, George E) with 211 records and James Drilling Company (Keaton, Michael K.) with 123. Historical record counts do not establish who is currently available or suited to your parcel.

sections.heading: Budget beyond the drilled hole in Wheat Ridge
sections.html:
The supplied cost model assumes Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock and a drilling rate of $50–$70 per foot. At the 30-foot median depth, that puts the drilled hole around $1,500–$2,100. The modeled finished well, including pump, tank, trenching and electrical, is approximately $7,500–$14,100.

That is a planning estimate, not a parcel quote. The 20–70-foot middle depth range gives useful context for footage allowances, but the mix of monitoring wells and deeper completions limits its value for a new household well. Have the bid identify the target formation, casing and grout, testing, access requirements and what happens financially if additional drilling is needed.

sections.heading: Environmental records deserve a closer look here
sections.html:
Within about 10 miles, the map includes 588 PFAS sampling/contamination sites, 144 historic mine features and 175 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites. Those counts flag places to investigate; they do not mean a particular Wheat Ridge well is contaminated. A sampling location is not automatically a confirmed contamination source.

Before buying, obtain laboratory water testing and ask the local health department which additional contaminants warrant attention at that address. Review nearby site records alongside the well’s construction and aquifer. Also inspect the wellhead and surface drainage, and confirm septic setbacks and buildable space. For a new well, discuss low-yield or unsuccessful drilling contingencies before equipment arrives.

sections.heading: Buying in Applewood or building near Fairmount
sections.html:
Start with the parcel’s DWR permit, construction report and available pumping-test records. A nearby well in Applewood or Fairmount is useful evidence only if its geology, construction and use resemble your proposed supply. The broad Wheat Ridge search radius also includes Lakeside, Mountain View and Edgewater, where records may serve very different purposes.

Confirm the permit allows the intended household and outdoor uses; an exempt household-use permit is not blanket irrigation permission. Where applicable, augmentation requirements can affect feasibility. Before closing or fixing the house location, coordinate well access, septic placement, driveway grading and utility trenches. Make a satisfactory water-supply review part of the purchase decision, not an afterthought.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Wheat Ridge, Colorado?
faq.a: Within 5 miles of Wheat Ridge, reported well depths have a 30-foot median, with the middle half between 20 and 70 feet. However, monitoring represents 42% of the use mix, so those figures are not exclusively household wells. Compare nearby domestic-well construction reports before using the median to budget for your property.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Wheat Ridge?
faq.a: The supplied bedrock cost model uses $50–$70 per foot. At the 30-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $1,500–$2,100, while a finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is about $7,500–$14,100. Actual bids need to address the parcel’s target aquifer, required depth, construction details and equipment access.

faq.q: How much water do Wheat Ridge wells produce?
faq.a: The 407 records reporting pump yield have a median of 10.0 gpm, and the middle half falls between 7.0 and 14.0 gpm. Under 1 gpm accounts for 3% of reported yields. For a purchase, request a pumping test that evaluates sustained supply; a historical yield entry does not guarantee current performance.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Wheat Ridge?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from depth or nearby permit records. The surrounding mapped area includes 588 PFAS sampling/contamination sites and 175 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites within about 10 miles, but proximity alone does not establish contamination. Obtain laboratory testing for the property and consult the local health department about testing guided by nearby environmental records.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Wheat Ridge?
faq.a: The available decade medians do not show a steady decline. Median depth to water was 95 feet in the 1970s, compared with 14 feet in the 2010s and 11 feet in the 2020s. These grouped records cover different wells, so they cannot establish a parcel-level trend. Review repeated measurements from the well you intend to use.
